title: Maghi: the torn letter
hookLine: at Muktsar the story of the forty and their torn letter is told again

cards: The sound of paper tearing is small. A quick rip, and it's done. But Sikh memory has kept one tear for a very long time.

At Muktsar, in Punjab, on the winter day called Maghi, crowds come to the pool and the gurdwaras of the town, and the story is told again: Sikhs who signed a paper walking away from their Guru, then came back and fell in battle, and the Guru who tore that paper up.

teach.b: During the siege of Anandpur, tradition says, a band of Sikhs asked to go home, and the Guru asked them to write it down. They signed a disclaimer, the bedava: you are not our Guru, we are not your Sikhs.
A paper is a record. It can outlast the mood that wrote it. Shamed and stirred by Mai Bhago, the same men rode back and fell at Khidrana, defending the Guru.
Tradition says one of them, Mahan Singh, was still alive when the Guru reached him, and asked for one thing: tear up the paper.
The Guru tore it. The record was gone. The relationship was whole.
The Ardas names them as the Chali Mukte, the liberated ones, and tradition ties the town's name, Muktsar, to them.

On Ang 1372, Bhagat Kabir says, in paraphrase, that where there is wisdom there is dharam, where there is falsehood there is sin, where there is greed there is death, and where there is forgiveness, there is the Lord himself.
On that reading, the Guru's tear wasn't a small kindness at the end of a battle.

It was the Lord's own presence in a torn page. Maghi could have been a day about loyalty, about the ones who never left. Instead, the story it tells is about people who left, came back, and were forgiven.

how: On Maghi, Sikhs gather at Sri Muktsar Sahib to bathe in the pool, visit the town's gurdwaras and hear kirtan, and the story of the Chali Mukte and the torn disclaimer is retold. Gurdwaras elsewhere also remember them.

games.q: you're Mahan Singh, wounded at Khidrana, and the Guru is beside you. he asks what you wish for. what do you ask?
o: to have the paper torn up.
to have your name written in a book.
games.why: he asked for the bedava to be torn, and tradition says the Guru tore it.

practice: On any scrap of paper, a receipt or a sticky note, write a word or two that stands for an old grudge you've kept; nobody will see it.

Hold it for a breath, then tear it slowly in half, and in half again, knowing you don't have to feel finished with it, since tearing is only a start. Set the pieces aside and breathe slowly, and if you pray, you can say Waheguru.
